title: Stars and bars
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Stars for the things, bars for the splits. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $[[n]]$ identical sweets be shared among $[[k]]$ children, if a child may get none?

mistakes.why: That gives every child at least one. Here a child may get none.

hints: Use $[[n]]$ stars and $[[k - 1]]$ bars: a row of $[[n + k - 1]]$ symbols.
Choose where the bars go.

problems.prompt: How many solutions does $a + b + c = [[n]]$ have in positive integers?

mistakes.why: That allows zeros. Each of $a$, $b$, $c$ must be at least $1$.

hints: Give each variable $1$ first. Then share the remaining $[[n - 3]]$ freely.

problems.prompt: How many solutions does $a + b + c + d = [[n]]$ have in whole numbers $a, b, c, d \geq 0$?

mistakes.why: That needs each variable to be at least $1$. Here zeros are allowed.

hints: $[[n]]$ stars and $3$ bars.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $[[n]]$ identical balls be put into $3$ different boxes, with at least $2$ balls in each box?

mistakes.why: Put $2$ balls in each box first, then share what is left.

hints: After $2$ in each box, $[[n - 6]]$ balls are left to share freely.

problems.prompt: A shop sells $[[k]]$ kinds of doughnut. In how many ways can you buy $[[n]]$ doughnuts? (Only how many of each kind matters.)

mistakes.why: That counts the doughnuts in order. Only the number of each kind matters.

hints: The $[[n]]$ doughnuts are the stars; $[[k - 1]]$ bars split them into kinds.

title: Stars and bars challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $8$ identical apples be shared among $3$ children, if a child may get none?

why.A: That gives every child at least one apple.

problems.prompt: How many solutions does $a + b + c + d = 9$ have in positive integers?
problems.solution: Give each $1$, then share $5$ among $4$: $\binom{8}{3} = 56$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: A shop sells $5$ kinds of doughnut. In how many ways can you buy $4$ doughnuts, if only how many of each kind matters?

why.E: Order doesn't matter here, only how many of each kind.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $10$ identical balls go into $4$ different boxes with at least $2$ balls in each box?

why.E: That only puts at least $1$ in each box.

problems.solution: Put $2$ in each box ($8$ balls), then share the last $2$ among $4$ boxes: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many solutions does $a + b + c = 10$ have in whole numbers $a, b, c \geq 0$ with $a \leq 3$?

why.A: That counts the solutions with $a \geq 4$, the ones to leave out.

title: Inclusion–exclusion
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Add the sets, then take away the overlap. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, [[n]]$ are divisible by $[[a]]$ or by $[[b]]$?

mistakes.why: The multiples of $[[a*b]]$ were counted twice. Take them away once.

hints: Count the multiples of $[[a]]$, of $[[b]]$, and of both (multiples of $[[a*b]]$).

problems.prompt: In a class of $[[n]]$, $[[x]]$ students play football, $[[y]]$ play tennis and $[[z]]$ play both. How many play neither?

mistakes.why: The $[[z]]$ who play both were taken away twice. Add them back once.

hints: At least one sport: $[[x]] + [[y]] - [[z]]$.
problems.solution: $[[x]] + [[y]] - [[z]] = [[x + y - z]]$ play at least one, so $[[n]] - [[x + y - z]] = [[n - x - y + z]]$ play neither.

problems.prompt: Set $A$ has $[[a]]$ members, set $B$ has $[[b]]$ members, and together they have $[[u]]$ different members. How many members are in both?
hints: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, [[n]]$ are divisible by neither $2$ nor $3$?

mistakes.why: The multiples of $6$ were taken away twice. Add them back once.

hints: First count those divisible by $2$ or $3$, then take that from $[[n]]$.
problems.solution: Divisible by $2$ or $3$: $[[floor(n/2)]] + [[floor(n/3)]] - [[floor(n/6)]] = [[floor(n/2) + floor(n/3) - floor(n/6)]]$. Neither: $[[n]] - [[floor(n/2) + floor(n/3) - floor(n/6)]] = [[n - floor(n/2) - floor(n/3) + floor(n/6)]]$.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, [[n]]$ are divisible by at least one of $2$, $3$ and $5$?

mistakes.why: The multiples of $30$ were added three times and taken away three times. Add them back once.

hints: Singles: multiples of $2$, $3$, $5$. Pairs: of $6$, $10$, $15$. Triple: of $30$.

title: Inclusion–exclusion challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 100$ are divisible by $2$ or by $5$?

why.D: The multiples of $10$ were counted twice.

problems.prompt: In a class of $30$, $18$ students like maths, $15$ like art and $8$ like both. How many like neither?
How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 1000$ are divisible by neither $2$ nor $3$?

why.E: That counts the numbers divisible by $2$ or $3$.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 300$ are divisible by at least one of $3$, $4$ and $5$?

why.E: Numbers in two of the sets were counted twice.

problems.prompt: The numbers $1, 2, 3, 4$ are put in a row in random order. In how many orders is no number in its own place (so $1$ is not first, $2$ is not second, and so on)?
problems.solution: All orders $24$. Take away those with a given number fixed: $4 \times 3! = 24$. Add back two fixed: $6 \times 2! = 12$. Take away three fixed: $4 \times 1 = 4$. Add back all four: $1$. $24 - 24 + 12 - 4 + 1 = 9$, choice (C).

title: Probability
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Write each probability as a fraction in lowest terms. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is $[[s]]$?

mistakes.why: The $11$ sums are not equally likely. Count the $36$ ordered pairs.

hints: List the ordered pairs that add to $[[s]]$.
There are $36$ equally likely pairs.
problems.solution: $[[6 - abs(s - 7)]]$ of the $36$ pairs add to $[[s]]$, so the probability is $[[(6 - abs(s - 7))/36]]$.

problems.prompt: A whole number is chosen at random from $1$ to $[[n]]$. What is the probability that it is a multiple of $[[d]]$?
hints: There are $[[floor(n/d)]]$ multiples of $[[d]]$ up to $[[n]]$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly $[[k]]$ heads?

mistakes.why: That is one outcome. There are $\binom{[[n]]}{[[k]]}$ ways to choose which coins are heads.

hints: There are $2^{[[n]]}$ equally likely outcomes.
Choose which $[[k]]$ coins land heads.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of at least one head?

mistakes.why: That is the chance of NO heads. Subtract it from $1$.

hints: The opposite of "at least one head" is "all tails".

problems.prompt: A bag holds $[[a]]$ red and $[[b]]$ blue marbles. Two are taken out without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are red?

mistakes.why: That puts the first marble back. Without it, the second draw has one fewer red and one fewer marble.

hints: First red: $\frac{[[a]]}{[[a + b]]}$. Then second red: $\frac{[[a - 1]]}{[[a + b - 1]]}$.

title: Probability challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: A letter is chosen at random from the word PROBABILITY. What is the probability that it is a B?

why.E: Count every letter, repeats included: there are $11$.

problems.solution: $2$ of the $11$ letters are B: $\frac{2}{11}$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is $9$?
Three fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly two heads?

why.B: The four possible numbers of heads aren't equally likely.

problems.solution: HHT, HTH, THH: $3$ of the $8$ outcomes, $\frac{3}{8}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A bag holds $4$ red and $6$ blue marbles. Two are taken out at once. What is the probability that they are different colours?

why.C: That puts the first marble back before the second draw.

problems.prompt: Three different numbers are chosen at random from $1, 2, \ldots, 10$. What is the probability that their product is even?
problems.solution: The product is odd only if all three are odd: $\frac{\binom{5}{3}}{\binom{10}{3}} = \frac{10}{120} = \frac{1}{12}$. So even: $1 - \frac{1}{12} = \frac{11}{12}$, choice (D).

title: Geometric probability
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Shade the good part and compare lengths or areas. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: A number $x$ is chosen at random between $0$ and $[[l]]$. What is the probability that $x < [[a]]$?
hints: The good part is from $0$ to $[[a]]$, out of a total length $[[l]]$.

problems.prompt: A number $x$ is chosen at random between $0$ and $[[l]]$. What is the probability that $x$ is closer to $0$ than to $[[c]]$?

mistakes.why: Closer to $0$ means left of the halfway point $\frac{[[c]]}{2}$, not left of $[[c]]$.

hints: $x$ is closer to $0$ when it is less than the halfway point between $0$ and $[[c]]$.
problems.solution: The good part is from $0$ to $\frac{[[c]]}{2}$, so the probability is $\frac{[[c]]}{2 \times [[l]]} = [[c/(2*l)]]$.

problems.prompt: A point is chosen at random inside a $[[a]] \times [[b]]$ rectangle. A $[[c]] \times [[c]]$ square is drawn inside the rectangle. What is the probability that the point lands in the square?

mistakes.why: Use the square's area, $[[c]]^2 = [[c^2]]$, not its side.

hints: Compare areas: $[[c^2]]$ out of $[[a*b]]$.

problems.prompt: A point $(x, y)$ is chosen at random in the square with corners $(0, 0)$ and $([[s]], [[s]])$. What is the probability that $x + y < [[t]]$?

mistakes.why: The good region is a triangle: its area is half of $[[t]] \times [[t]]$.

hints: The good region is the triangle with corners $(0, 0)$, $([[t]], 0)$ and $(0, [[t]])$.
problems.solution: The triangle has area $\frac{[[t]]^2}{2} = [[t^2/2]]$ and the square $[[s^2]]$, so the probability is $[[t^2/(2*s^2)]]$.

problems.prompt: A dart lands at a random point on a round board of radius $[[b]]$. What is the probability that it lands within $[[a]]$ of the centre?

mistakes.why: Compare areas, not radii: areas grow with the square of the radius.

hints: The good region is a circle of radius $[[a]]$: area $[[a^2]]\pi$.

title: Geometric probability challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: A point is chosen at random on a segment of length $12$. What is the probability that it is at least $3$ away from both ends?
problems.solution: The good part is the middle $12 - 6 = 6$: $\frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A point is chosen at random inside a $6 \times 6$ square. What is the probability that it lies inside the circle that touches all four sides?
problems.solution: The circle has radius $3$ and area $9\pi$; the square has area $36$. $\frac{9\pi}{36} = \frac{\pi}{4}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A number $x$ is chosen at random between $0$ and $10$. What is the probability that $x$ is closer to $3$ than to $8$?

why.A: The good part runs to the halfway point between $3$ and $8$, not to $3$.

problems.solution: The halfway point is $5.5$. Every $x$ below it is closer to $3$: $\frac{5.5}{10} = \frac{11}{20}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A point $(x, y)$ is chosen at random in the square with corners $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 4)$. What is the probability that $x + y < 3$?

why.E: The good region is a triangle: half of $3 \times 3$.

problems.solution: The triangle has area $\frac{9}{2}$ and the square $16$: $\frac{9}{32}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Two numbers $x$ and $y$ are chosen at random between $0$ and $1$. What is the probability that $|x - y| < \frac{1}{2}$?

why.A: That is the chance they are MORE than $\frac{1}{2}$ apart.

problems.solution: In the unit square, the bad region is two corner triangles, each of area $\frac{1}{8}$. So the probability is $1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$, choice (D).

title: Expected value
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Weight each value by its probability, then add. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: A fair die has $[[n]]$ faces numbered $1$ to $[[n]]$. What is the expected value of one roll?

mistakes.why: The average of $1, 2, \ldots, [[n]]$ is $\frac{1 + [[n]]}{2}$.

hints: Add the faces: $1 + 2 + \cdots + [[n]] = [[n*(n + 1)/2]]$. Then divide by $[[n]]$.

problems.prompt: A spinner pays $[[a]]$ points with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, $[[b]]$ points with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, and $0$ points with probability $\frac{1}{4}$. What is the expected number of points?

mistakes.why: The three results aren't equally likely. Weight each by its probability.

hints: $E = \frac{1}{2} \times [[a]] + \frac{1}{4} \times [[b]] + \frac{1}{4} \times 0$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the expected value of their total?

mistakes.why: One die averages $\frac{7}{2}$, not $3$.

hints: Expected values add. One die averages $\frac{7}{2}$.

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled $[[n]]$ times. What is the expected number of sixes?
hints: Each roll is a six with probability $\frac{1}{6}$. Add up over the $[[n]]$ rolls.

problems.prompt: A jar holds $[[a]]$ one-cent coins, $[[b]]$ five-cent coins and $[[c]]$ ten-cent coins. One coin is taken at random. What is its expected value in cents?

mistakes.why: The three kinds of coin aren't equally likely. Weight each by how many there are.

hints: The total value is $[[a + 5*b + 10*c]]$ cents, spread over $[[a + b + c]]$ coins.

title: Expected value challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: What is the expected value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?

why.E: Divide the total by the $6$ faces.

problems.prompt: You flip a fair coin. Heads, you win $10$ points; tails, you lose $4$ points. What is your expected gain?

why.E: Tails costs you $4$ points: subtract, don't add.

problems.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the expected value of the product of the two numbers?
problems.solution: The dice are independent, so the expected product is $\frac{7}{2} \times \frac{7}{2} = \frac{49}{4}$, choice (D).

problems.prompt: A box has $3$ red and $2$ blue balls. Two balls are taken out without putting back. What is the expected number of red balls taken?

why.A: That is for one draw. Expected values add over the two draws.

problems.solution: Each draw is red with probability $\frac{3}{5}$, so the expected number is $2 \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{6}{5}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled until a $6$ appears. What is the expected number of rolls?
problems.solution: Let $E$ be the answer. One roll is always made; with probability $\frac{5}{6}$ you start again. $E = 1 + \frac{5}{6}E$, so $E = 6$, choice (D).

title: ⭐ Unit 10 check
instructions: Eight AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first, no hints. You need all 8 right to pass. Each try gives you different problems.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $6$ identical cookies be shared among $3$ children, if a child may get none?

why.A: That gives every child at least one.
why.E: The cookies are identical, so their order doesn't matter.

problems.prompt: How many solutions does $a + b + c = 12$ have in positive integers?
A bakery sells $4$ kinds of bagel. In how many ways can you buy $6$ bagels with at least one of each kind?

why.E: That ignores "at least one of each kind".

problems.solution: Take one of each kind, then choose $2$ more from $4$ kinds: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 60$ are divisible by $4$ or by $6$?

why.D: The multiples of $12$ were counted twice.

problems.prompt: Of $40$ students, $22$ study French, $18$ study Spanish and $7$ study neither. How many study both?
How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, [[n]]$ are divisible by $2$ or by $3$?

why.B: The multiples of $6$ were counted twice.
why.D: That counts the numbers divisible by neither.

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 120$ share no factor greater than $1$ with $30$?
problems.solution: Take away multiples of $2$, $3$, $5$ by inclusion–exclusion: $120 - 60 - 40 - 24 + 20 + 12 + 8 - 4 = 32$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is $10$?
A card is drawn at random from cards numbered $1$ to $20$. What is the probability that its number is prime?

why.B: Did you leave out $2$? It is prime.

problems.prompt: Four fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly two heads?

why.B: The five possible numbers of heads aren't equally likely.

problems.prompt: A bag holds $5$ red and $3$ green marbles. Two are taken out without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are green?

why.B: That puts the first marble back.

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled three times. What is the probability that at least one roll is a $6$?

why.C: Adding $\frac{1}{6}$ three times counts the outcomes with two or three sixes more than once.
why.D: That is the chance of NO six.

problems.solution: No six: $\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^3 = \frac{125}{216}$. At least one: $1 - \frac{125}{216} = \frac{91}{216}$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: A point is chosen at random on a segment of length $10$. What is the probability that it is within $2$ of the midpoint?

why.A: Within $2$ means $2$ on EITHER side of the midpoint.

problems.solution: The good part has length $4$: $\frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A dart lands at a random point on a round board of radius $6$. What is the probability that it lands within $2$ of the centre?
A point is chosen at random in the square with corners $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 2)$. What is the probability that it is at most $1$ away from $(0, 0)$?

why.D: Only a quarter of the circle is inside the square, and the square has area $4$.

problems.solution: The good region is a quarter circle of radius $1$, area $\frac{\pi}{4}$. The square has area $4$: $\frac{\pi}{16}$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: A spinner has four equal sections labelled $1$, $2$, $3$ and $10$. What is the expected value of one spin?
You pay $3$ points to roll a fair die, and then win as many points as the number rolled. What is your expected gain?
$[[n]]$ fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the expected value of their total?
Four boys and four girls stand in a row in random order. What is the expected number of neighbouring pairs made of one boy and one girl?
problems.solution: Each of the $7$ neighbouring pairs is mixed with probability $\frac{4}{8} \times \frac{4}{7} \times 2 = \frac{4}{7}$. Expected values add: $7 \times \frac{4}{7} = 4$, choice (D).
